title: In Their Own Words
notes: You asked for Einstein specifically, but I left him out — the “Information is not knowledge, the only source of knowledge is experience” line usually pinned on him is confirmed misattributed (the Einstein Archives have no record of it; it traces to Frank Zappa in 1979, not Einstein). I swapped in Sherman Kent instead, who's arguably a better fit anyway — he's literally called “the father of intelligence analysis” and spent 17 years at the CIA formalizing the discipline.

Every quote here (center and the scattered edge fragments) is independently verified against a primary or authoritative source, not pulled from a quote-aggregator site and trusted blindly: Sun Tzu's Art of War (multiple chapters), Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching, George Washington's actual 1777 letter to Col. Elias Dayton (via the Library of Congress / Founders Archives), Sherman Kent's 1949 book, Churchill's remark at the Tehran Conference (authentic, though possibly based on an older Russian proverb — noted for completeness), and Francis Bacon's 1597 “Meditationes Sacrae” (his real original wording — the famous Latin “scientia potentia est” is actually Thomas Hobbes', not Bacon's).

title: The Mission
notes: Colonel John Boyd, a USAF fighter pilot and strategist, developed it after studying why American F-86 pilots consistently beat the technically superior MiG-15 in Korea: not better hardware, but faster decision cycles. He formalized the idea in his 1976 essay "Destruction and Creation" and his 1986 briefing "Patterns of Conflict." The core claim: whoever cycles through Observe → Orient → Decide → Act faster than their opponent can react is effectively always fighting yesterday's situation — they're "behind the loop."

Intelligence's role: the "Orient" step is where a decision-maker's mental model of the situation gets built, and that model is only as good as the intelligence feeding it. Bad or late intelligence doesn't just slow the loop down, it corrupts it — the commander acts confidently on wrong information. That's the strongest answer if anyone asks "why does this job matter": intel officers are the input to the fastest possible decision cycle, not just people filing reports.

title: Two Tracks, One Mission
notes: You commission via AFROTC, OTS, or USAFA — that line got trimmed off the card since your own path (AFROTC) already makes it obvious, but it's worth having ready if asked.

One fact that got cut when the career-progression slide was removed, and is worth keeping in your back pocket: new officers commission as O-1 (2nd Lieutenant) and promote automatically through O-3 (Captain) based on time in service — no board required until Major (O-4). Say the word if you want a rank-timeline slide added back in.

Also useful for Q&A: "14N" and "1N0X1" are Air Force Specialty Codes (AFSCs). The 14-series is officer-level; 1N is intelligence enlisted. The "N" doesn't abbreviate anything specific — it's just the assigned career-field letter.

title: Raw Data → Usable Intel
notes: SIMPLIFIED to 5:6 and 7: TechINT, and CI – CI is OSI mission. A little more depth on each, useful if someone asks a follow-up question:
SIGINT splits into two sub-types: COMINT (intercepted communications) and ELINT (non-communication signals, like radar emissions).
GEOINT is run nationally by the NGA (National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency) and is broader than "satellite photos" — it includes mapping, terrain data, and anything imagery-derived.
HUMINT is by far the oldest form of intelligence (older than any technology-based INT) and includes legitimate liaison/diplomatic contacts, not just clandestine sources.

MASINT is the least well-known INT outside the community — it's about technical signatures rather than content: recognizing a specific radar or engine by its electronic "fingerprint" rather than intercepting what it's saying.
OSINT has grown enormously because of social media and commercial satellite imagery — a lot of what used to require classified collection is now publicly purchasable or scrapable.

Why the slide now says "five MAIN collection disciplines": the Air Force's own 14N career-field documentation lists SIX disciplines - these five plus TECHINT (technical intelligence, the exploitation of captured or acquired foreign equipment). Joint doctrine (JP 2-0) lists SEVEN by adding counterintelligence (CI), though in the Air Force CI is an OSI mission, not a 14N one. "Five" is a recruiting-page simplification, so if anyone pushes on the number, that is the answer - and it shows you read the career-field standard rather than the brochure.

title: Putting It Together
notes: The formal DoD definition (Joint Publication 2-0): all-source intelligence is intelligence products, organizations, and activities that incorporate all sources of information — HUMINT, GEOINT, MASINT, SIGINT, and OSINT — into one finished product. That's the actual doctrinal wording, not slide paraphrase.

One tradecraft detail that shows real understanding if it comes up: analysts commonly grade a source's reliability and a specific report's credibility separately (a reliable source can still report something implausible, and vice versa). A well-known framework for this is the NATO "Admiralty System," which rates source reliability A–F and information credibility 1–6 (e.g. "B2" = usually reliable source, probably true information). You don't need this on the slide — it's just a good answer if someone asks "how do they know what to trust?"

title: Getting There
notes: "Tier 5 Investigation" used to be called an SSBI (Single Scope Background Investigation) — same process, renamed. It's the deepest level of federal background investigation, required for Top Secret access and anything involving Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI).

It covers roughly the last 10 years of your life: every address, employer, school, foreign contact, and financial record, verified through record checks plus in-person interviews — including an "Enhanced Subject Interview" with you directly, and interviews with people who know you personally and professionally. That's genuinely why it takes as long as it does - it's real investigative legwork, not paperwork sitting on a desk. On timing: the slide used to say 12–24 months, which reflected the old clearance backlog and now reads as out of date. Current published processing figures put Top Secret commonly under a year, with TS/SCI (which adds SCI indoctrination and sometimes a polygraph) running longer. The honest driver of variance is your own background - foreign contacts, foreign travel, finances, dual citizenship - not paperwork speed.

SEIs (Special Experience Identifiers) are a tracking code the Air Force uses to flag who's had extra training beyond their base AFSC — they're not separate jobs, just tags that make someone eligible for specialized taskings.

title: From Commissioning To The Squadron
notes: IOT (Intelligence Officer Training) at Goodfellow AFB is the shared starting point for every 14N regardless of what they'll eventually support — it teaches the common foundation: tradecraft, briefing skills, basic threat analysis.

After that, "follow-on training" is where it branches hard: a 14N headed to a fighter squadron trains differently than one headed to an RPA (drone) unit, a space unit, or an intelligence production center — the course is tailored to whatever platform or mission they're actually assigned to.

"Operations Group" is the standard organizational layer at a flying wing — it sits under the Wing Commander and owns the flying squadrons directly. That's where a 14N is typically embedded, not off in a separate intel-only unit.

title: Beyond The Baseline
notes: Speciality/specialization tracks:These four aren't separate entry-level jobs — they're where the career field branches after someone is already qualified (an SEI for officers, a follow-on award for enlisted).

Targeting (1N8X1) is generally the most kinetic / operationally direct specialty — its product can directly feed a strike decision, which also means it carries the heaviest weight of responsibility in the field.

Collection management is less a separate specialty than a skill experienced analysts grow into — deciding where to point limited collection assets is one of the hardest judgment calls in intelligence, because there's never enough collection capacity to answer every open question.

title: On The Job
notes: Worth knowing for Q&A: a lot of real-world intel work happens in a SCIF (Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility) — a secure, access-controlled space where classified material can be discussed and processed.

Ops tempo is genuinely shift-based rather than 9-to-5. Units supporting real-time or combat operations often run their intelligence shop 24/7 in rotating shifts, which is a different rhythm than a lot of other Air Force jobs.

title: Bigger Picture
notes: MAJCOM examples worth naming if asked: ACC (Air Combat Command, fighters/ISR), AMC (Air Mobility Command, airlift/tankers), AFSOC (Air Force Special Operations Command), PACAF (Pacific Air Forces) — each sets its own intelligence priorities within DoD-wide requirements.

On the national agencies: NASIC (National Air and Space Intelligence Center) is headquartered at Wright-Patterson AFB in Ohio. Its job is analyzing foreign air, space, missile, and cyber threats, and it actually traces its lineage back to WWII, when captured enemy aircraft were studied at that same base. DIA (Defense Intelligence Agency) is the overall DoD-wide intelligence agency — NASIC feeds it specialized air-threat analysis. NSA (National Security Agency) runs the nation's signals intelligence collection and also holds the government's primary cybersecurity mission. None of these three are Air Force-only — they're joint/national organizations — but Air Force intelligence people feed them and draw on their products constantly.
